claims.text: The proposed starting material is a nanoscale multilayer coating of alternating FCC and BCC HEA layers with low initial short-range order and intact coherent interfaces.
Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading is governed by stress-induced evolution of chemical short-range order at nanoscale interfaces.
Stress-induced short-range ordering gradually reduces interfacial dislocation pinning.
Reduced interfacial pinning enhances dislocation mobility through glide and climb.
The intervention is constant sub-yield loading at elevated temperature, optionally preceded by controlled aging to alter short-range order.
Aging can increase chemical ordering in an HEA.
Evolution of local chemical order at multilayer interfaces alters interfacial cohesion and dislocation barrier heights.
Under sustained mechanical loading, lattice distortion and compositional complexity drive gradual atomic reordering at interfaces.
Increased short-range order lowers resistance to dislocation motion.
Increased short-range order promotes dislocation climb and glide.
Developing short-range order progressively reduces barriers to dislocation transfer between layers.
Reduced barriers to interlayer dislocation transfer cause an accelerating creep strain rate.
Multilayers that develop enhanced short-range order, or are pre-aged to induce it, should have a higher creep strain rate than a random-order baseline.
More highly ordered interfacial regions should spatially correlate with dislocation activity.
Random chemical order and strong coherent interfaces provide effective dislocation impediments and therefore a lower creep strain rate.
The hypothesis is restricted to conditions in which multilayer periodicity is retained and grain-boundary sliding or dynamic recrystallization does not dominate.

The magnitude and composition or layer-thickness dependence of the proposed creep-rate change are uncertain because competing processes such as recrystallization or interface decohesion may contribute.

Failure to observe a statistically significant increase in creep rate and dislocation mobility in the higher-SRO group, or failure to observe a correlation between SRO and deformation, would falsify the hypothesis.
